chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding a man who kills a woman intentionally: If the woman's family wishes to kill him, he tells them: Do so, provided they pay to his family half the blood money. And if they accept the blood money, then they receive half the blood money.

Second: Ali, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Musa, from Abdullah ibn Maskan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: If a man kills a woman, and they want qisas (retaliation), they pay the difference in the man's blood money and retaliate with it. And if they do not do so, they accept the blood money as a complete payment, and the woman's blood money is half that of the man's.

Third: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) say regarding a man who intentionally kills his wife: If her family wishes to kill him, they pay to him half the blood money. And if they wish, they take half the blood money, which is five thousand dirhams.

Fourth: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn al-Jabbar, from Safwan, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, from Abu Baseer, from one of the Imams (peace be upon him) who said: I asked: A man kills a woman? He said: If the woman's family wishes to kill him, they pay half his blood money and kill him. Otherwise, they accept the blood money.

Fifth: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Mufaddal, from Zayd al-Shahham, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), regarding a man who intentionally kills a woman: He said: If her family wishes to kill him, they kill him and pay to him half the blood money.

Sixth: As for what al-Saffar narrated from al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Khashshab, from Ghiyath ibn Kalub, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), that a man killed a woman and Ali (peace be upon him) did not establish qisas between them but obligated the blood money: This does not contradict the earlier reports for two reasons: First, it is permissible that he did not establish qisas between them because the killing was not intentional, which requires qisas. Second, he did not establish qisas between them, so there is no need to return the difference in blood money, because the earlier reports included that there is qisas between them on the condition that they return the difference of her blood money to the man's guardians. So whenever they do not return it, they have only the blood money. And that which confirms this:

Seventh: What Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Abu Ja'far, from Abu al-Jawza', from al-Husayn ibn Alwan, from Amr ibn Khalid, from Zayd ibn Ali, from his fathers, from Ali (peace be upon him) who said: There is no qisas between the man and the women except in the soul. So he established qisas between them in the soul on the condition we mentioned. As for what this report included that there is no qisas between them except in the soul, the meaning is that there is no qisas between them in which the man and the woman are equal, because the blood money of the woman's limbs is half that of the man's limbs, if it exceeds what is one-third of the blood money, as we explained in al-Kitab al-Kabir. And that which indicates that qisas is established between them in the limbs:

Eighth: What al-Hasan ibn Mahbub narrated from Abdullah ibn Sayyab, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said: Indeed, in the book of Ali (peace be upon him): If a man cuts the private part of his wife, he is liable to pay her her blood money. If he does not pay her her blood money, I will cut her private part if she requests that.
ai.seo_question: What is the blood money and retaliation rule when a man kills a woman in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: These hadiths from al-Istibsar elucidate the Shia jurisprudence of qisas (retaliation) and diya (blood money) for intentional homicide, establishing that while a man and woman are equal in the right to life, the financial compensation for a woman is half that of a man. The texts resolve apparent contradictions by clarifying that if the victim's family chooses qisas, they must pay the 'excess' diya (the difference between the man's and woman's diya) to the killer's heirs, a nuance confirmed by Ali ibn Abi Talib’s judicial practice. This framework ensures that the principle of equality in the soul is balanced with the established disparity in financial liability for limbs and life.
